overview.text: Painted by Spanish artist Pablo Picasso in Paris in 1907, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon is a monumental oil painting of five nude women arranged tightly in a shallow, fractured space. Their angular bodies, flattened planes, and strikingly different faces reject the smooth anatomy and single viewpoint expected in much European painting. Picasso drew on varied artistic sources, including Iberian sculpture and African and Oceanic objects; the ways he appropriated these works are also part of the painting’s cultural history. Often described as proto-Cubist and a landmark of modern art, it helped set a radical direction for Picasso’s experiments, though scholars debate whether it is itself Cubist. Its title refers to a Barcelona street associated with sex work, not the French city of Avignon.

key_facts.text: The oil-on-canvas work measures about 244 by 234 centimeters (8 feet by 7 feet 8 inches).
The title, given around the time of the painting’s first public exhibition, refers to a Barcelona street associated with the city’s red-light district.
Picasso made hundreds of preparatory drawings and studies while developing the painting.
The Philadelphia Museum of Art describes the painting as proto-Cubist; MoMA notes that whether it is Cubist remains debated.
MoMA connects the two rightmost figures’ stylized features to Picasso’s interest in African masks and sculpture, while also emphasizing that these objects reached France through colonial channels.
